s.f: \text{order}=\text{highest derivative};\quad\text{degree}=\text{power of the highest derivative (after making it polynomial in derivatives)}
s.n: Degree is not defined if derivatives appear inside $\sin$, $e^{(\cdot)}$, $\ln$ etc.
Order of the DE = number of independent arbitrary constants.

s.f: \text{general: has } n \text{ arbitrary constants};\quad\text{particular: constants fixed by initial conditions}

s.q: DE of all circles / parabolas families (orders)
s.f: \text{circles in a plane}: 3;\quad\text{circles through origin}: 2;\quad\text{parabolas with axis along } x\text{-axis}: 2

s.n: Reducible: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{a_1x+b_1y+c_1}{a_2x+b_2y+c_2}$ — shift origin $x=X+h,\ y=Y+k$ (if $\frac{a_1}{a_2}\ne\frac{b_1}{b_2}$), else put $v=a_1x+b_1y$.

s.d: Multiply by $e^{\int P}$: the left side becomes $\frac d{dx}\left(ye^{\int P}\right)$.

s.f: M\,dx+N\,dy=0\ \text{exact iff}\ \frac{\partial M}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}
P=\frac1x\Rightarrow\text{IF}=x;\quad P=-\frac1x\Rightarrow\frac1x;\quad P=\tan x\Rightarrow\sec x;\quad P=\cot x\Rightarrow\sin x

s.q: Curve whose tangent / normal has a property
s.f: \text{write the property with } y'\ \text{and solve the DE}

s.n: Equal roots: $(A+Bx)e^{mx}$; complex $\alpha\pm i\beta$: $e^{\alpha x}(A\cos\beta x+B\sin\beta x)$.

s.q: Maximum / value of the solution at a point
s.f: \text{solve fully, apply the initial condition, then evaluate or differentiate}

s: If this type comes, solve like this

s.q: If the equation is linear in $y$ after rearranging ($\frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)y=Q(x)$)
s.r: "$\cos x(3\sin x+\cos x+3)dy=(1+y\sin x(3\sin x+\cos x+3))dx$", "$(x-x^3)dy=(y+yx^2-3x^4)dx$", a long fraction multiplying $y$ that simplifies.
s.s: Divide to get the form $\frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)y=Q(x)$ (coefficient of $\frac{dy}{dx}$ equal to 1). || Find the integrating factor $e^{\int Pdx}$ (simplify $P$ with partial fractions or by spotting a derivative). || Multiply and integrate: $y\cdot\text{IF}=\int Q\cdot\text{IF}\,dx+C$. || Use the initial condition for $C$, then evaluate.
s.e: First example: $\frac{dy}{dx}-y\tan x=\frac{\sec x}{3\sin x+\cos x+3}$, IF $=\cos x$, so $y\cos x=\int\frac{dx}{3\sin x+\cos x+3}$.

s.q: If the equation is linear in $x$ (or in $\frac1{\ln\cos x}$) rather than in $y$
s.r: "$(\ln\cos y)^2\cos y\,dx-(1+3x\ln\cos y)\sin y\,dy=0$, solution $x=x(y)$", "$\cos x(\ln\cos x)^2dy+(\sin x-3y\sin x\ln\cos x)dx=0$".
s.s: If $x$ appears only to the first power, treat $x$ as the dependent variable and write $\frac{dx}{dy}+P(y)x=Q(y)$. || Integrating factor $e^{\int P(y)dy}$ (here a power of $\ln\cos y$). || Solve and use the given point.

s.q: If $f'=af+b$, or an integral equation reduces to a linear DE
s.s: For integral equations, multiply out the factor and differentiate both sides to get a DE. || Solve the linear DE. || Use the given value and limit to fix constants.

s.q: If the variables separate (possibly after partial fractions)
s.r: "$(x^2-4)dy-(y^2-3y)dx=0$", "$\frac{dy}{dx}=\ldots$ with a product of a function of $x$ and a function of $y$".
s.s: Bring all $y$ terms to one side and all $x$ terms to the other. || Use partial fractions: $\frac1{y(y-3)}=\frac13\left(\frac1{y-3}-\frac1y\right)$. || Integrate both sides; use the initial condition. || Solve for $y$ (watch the sign of the modulus from the initial point).

s.q: If the equation is homogeneous ($\frac{dy}{dx}=F(\frac yx)$)
s.s: Check that every term has the same total degree. || Put $y=vx$ and simplify: you get $x\frac{dv}{dx}=G(v)$. || Separate: $\int\frac{dv}{G(v)}=\int\frac{dx}x$. || Put $v=\frac yx$ back and use the initial condition. || Shortcut: $x\,dy-y\,dx$ means $d(\frac yx)$.

s.q: If it is homogeneous only after shifting the origin ($\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x+y-2}{x-y}$) or with $(x+2)$, $(y+1)$ blocks
s.f: X=x-h,\ Y=y-k\ \text{where the two lines meet}
s.s: Solve the numerator and denominator lines simultaneously to get $(h,k)$. || Shift: $X=x-h$, $Y=y-k$; the equation becomes homogeneous. || Put $Y=vX$ and solve. || Shift back.

s.q: If it is a Bernoulli equation ($\frac{dy}{dx}+Py=Qy^n$)
s.r: "$\frac{dy}{dx}=(y+1)\big((y+1)e^{x^2/2}-x\big)$", a power of $y$ (or of $y+1$) on the right.
s.s: Put $u=y+1$ if needed so it is $\frac{du}{dx}+Pu=Qu^n$. || Substitute $w=u^{1-n}$: the equation becomes linear in $w$. || Solve the linear equation, go back to $y$.

s.q: If the equation contains $(x+y)$ or $(x+y+c)$ as a block
s.s: Put $v$ = the block; then $\frac{dv}{dx}=1+\frac{dy}{dx}$. || The equation becomes separable or Bernoulli in $v$. || Solve and substitute back.

s.q: If tangent/normal geometry or an area condition gives the DE
s.r: "Tangent at $P$ meets the axes at $A$, $B$ with $P$ the midpoint", "slope of the tangent at $(x,y)$ is given", "area under $y=f(x)$ from 0 to $a$ is $e^{-a}+4a^2+a-1$".
s.s: Write the tangent (or normal) line at a general point $(x,y)$. || Express the given geometric condition (intercepts, distances, midpoint) as an equation in $x,y,y'$. || For area conditions, differentiate with respect to the upper limit. || Solve the DE with the given point.

s.q: If the order and degree, or the DE of a family of curves, is asked
s.r: "Degree − order for $y^2=a(x+\frac{\sqrt a}2)$", "DE of circles through the origin with centre on $y=x$", "parabolas with axis parallel to the y-axis and given latus rectum".
s.f: \text{order}=\text{number of independent constants};\ \ \text{degree: power of the highest derivative after removing radicals}
s.s: Count the arbitrary constants: that is the order. || Differentiate as many times and eliminate the constants. || Clear fractional powers of derivatives; the highest derivative's power is the degree.

s.q: If it is Newton's cooling or a growth/decay application
s.s: Separate: $\frac{dT}{T-T_s}=-Kdt$. || Use the given readings to find $K$. || Answer the time or temperature asked.

s.q: If an integral equation or a special condition defines the function (solve by differentiating)
s.s: Differentiate integral equations to get a DE. || Solve it with the conditions (oddness kills the $\cosh$ part). || Simplify trig of inverse trig first. || For limit definitions, the limit is a derivative; it gives a DE.
s.e: $\sqrt{1-y'^2}=y\Rightarrow y=\sin x$ up to $\frac\pi2$, then $y=1$; at $x=2$: $y''+y+1=2$. And $f=3\sinh x$ gives $9f(\ln3)=36$.
